The bottom button bar — your primary call-to-action and an optional secondary button. This guide documents every setting of the Action Bar block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

The Action Bar holds the screen's main call-to-action: the primary button (like Continue) and an optional secondary button. This is the control that actually moves visitors forward, so set its label to match what happens next and make sure it points to the same screen you connected on the canvas. It shows on most interactive screens; if a screen has no continuation button, add the next step from the canvas instead.
Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList, WebEmbed.

Sets the main button's look — background color, border, corner radius, height, inner padding, and a full-width toggle. For an ad landing page keep it full-width and high-contrast so it reads as the obvious next step. The Visibility toggle hides the button entirely; only hide it when the screen forces a choice first, and never hide both buttons.

Optional animation for the call-to-action — pulse, glow, bounce, scale, fade-in, slide-up and more, plus an opacity control. A gentle pulse or glow can draw the eye and lift taps; save attention-grabbing effects for your key conversion screen and avoid stacking several. Leave it off for a calm, professional feel.

An optional color gradient layered over the button's solid fill — set start and end colors, the angle, extra color stops, and an optional moving shimmer. Leave it off for a clean flat look; turn it on to make the call-to-action pop against a busy background. Keep enough contrast that the label stays easy to read.

An optional icon next to the label — choose start or end placement, size, corner radius, and spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). A small leading arrow or lock icon can reinforce the action; keep it in the same color family as the label. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

The text on your main call-to-action button — the one that moves visitors to the next screen. Make it a short, specific verb phrase tied to the action (Continue, Get my plan, Subscribe) rather than a generic word; clear, benefit-led labels lift click-through on a paid landing page. This text can be translated per language.

An optional drop shadow beneath the button, with control over its color, blur, and vertical drop. A soft shadow lifts the call-to-action off the page so it feels tappable; keep it subtle (low blur, small offset) so it looks intentional rather than heavy. Leave it off if your theme is flat.

Typography for the main button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Leave it on the theme defaults for a consistent look; bump the weight or size, or switch color, only when the label is hard to read against the button fill. Applies to the label in every language.

Sets the secondary button's look — background, border, corner radius, height, padding, and a full-width toggle. Give it lower visual weight than the main button (an outline or transparent fill works well) so it doesn't compete with your call-to-action. The Visibility toggle hides it; never hide both the primary and secondary buttons.

Adds optional movement to the secondary (lower-priority) button, such as pulse, glow, or bounce, plus an opacity control to fade it. Leave this off by default. Animation draws the eye, so reserve it for your main button only; making the alternative path move competes with your primary call to action and typically lowers conversions.

An optional color gradient over the secondary button's solid fill (start/end colors, angle, stops, optional shimmer). Usually leave this off — a gradient draws attention, which you want on your main call-to-action, not the side path. Turn it on only if a flat secondary clashes with your theme.

An optional icon on the secondary button — placement (start or end), size, corner radius, spacing, and how it fits its box (fit shows the whole icon, fill crops to cover). Usually leave it empty so the secondary stays understated; add one only when it clarifies the action, like a back arrow for Go back.

Text for the optional second button — use it for a side path like Skip, Maybe later, or Restore purchase, never your main goal. On funnel steps an easy escape route can cost conversions, so leave it empty unless you genuinely need the alternative; on a paywall a low-key secondary is fine.

An optional drop shadow under the secondary button (color, blur, vertical drop). Keep it lighter than the main button's shadow, or off entirely, so the secondary stays visually subordinate to your call-to-action.

Typography for the secondary button label — font, weight, size, color, and alignment. Style it deliberately quieter than the main button (lighter weight, muted color) so your primary call-to-action stays the obvious choice. Leave it on theme defaults unless the hierarchy looks off.

The number of seconds or minutes (unit chosen below) before the screen moves on by itself, from 1 to 300. Only used when auto-advance is on. Keep it short, about 2 to 4 seconds for a splash or 'analyzing...' screen, so visitors aren't left waiting and bouncing.

An auto-advancing slide deck — the slide template, total play time, each slide’s text and picture and timing, and the per-slide text/image styles. This guide documents every setting of the Carousel block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

Configures a Carousel screen — a set of slides (image plus optional text) that auto-advance on a timer to tell a quick visual story. Use it for a punchy intro, and keep slides few and fast so visitors reach the next step.
Covered screen types: Carousel.

Open this to override the third line's font size, weight, color, alignment, and the padding around it; it appears only with the Image + Title + 2 Subtitles template. Style it as the smallest, quietest text so it never competes with the headline or supporting line. Leave it on theme defaults unless you truly need a change, since overrides apply to this line on every slide of the carousel.

The total time in seconds for the whole carousel to play through once before it stops or the visitor moves on (0.1–120s). This total is split across slides by each slide's timing slider, so changing it speeds up or slows every slide proportionally. Start around 3–5 seconds per slide (about 12–20s for four slides) — long enough to read each line, short enough to keep momentum and avoid stalling the visitor.

Controls the box that holds each slide's image, separate from the image's own styling. Set how tall the box is (Auto fits the image, Fixed is an exact pixel height, Percent is a share of the slide), where the image sits inside it, and the padding around it. Leave it on Auto unless you want every slide's image to occupy the same vertical space so slides don't jump in size as visitors swipe.

Open this to control the slide image's width, height, corner radius, and how it fills its box: Fit shows the whole image (may leave bands), Fill covers the box (edges may crop), Crop trims to the exact box, and Tile repeats it. You also set the padding around the image. Fill is the usual choice for full-bleed slides and Fit keeps the whole graphic visible; settings apply to the image on every slide.

A third text line below the supporting line, available only with the Image + Title + 2 Subtitles template. Use it sparingly for one last small detail like a disclaimer or extra proof, since four text layers over an image quickly overcrowd a slide and slow reading. Supports @variable personalization, countdown timers, and styled chips, and is edited per language.

A two-thumb slider that sets the window, as a share of the carousel's total duration, during which this slide is on screen. Drag the thumbs apart to give this slide a longer share, which leaves less time for the others. For example, a 25% window at a 20-second total keeps this slide visible about 5 seconds; keep slides spread evenly and only widen the most persuasive one.

The image shown on this slide, required on every slide no matter which template you pick. Drag-and-drop or click to upload, and Segmently serves a fast-loading optimized version automatically. Use a high-quality picture that matches the slide's message; how it fills the slide is set in Image styles below, and a slide left without an image shows blank, so set one on every slide before publishing.

The line under the headline, shown only when the slide template is Image + Title + Subtitle or richer. Use it to back up the headline with a quick proof point or detail rather than repeat it. It supports @variable personalization, countdown timers, and styled chips, is edited per language, and only appears after you set a slide template that includes a subtitle.

The main headline on this slide, shown only when the slide template includes a title. Keep it short and benefit-led so it lands in the few seconds the slide is on screen. You can drop in the visitor's earlier answers with @variable, plus countdown timers and styled label chips; if your funnel runs in several languages, you edit this text per language.

Sets which layers each slide shows: Image Only is just the picture, Image + Title adds one headline, Image + Title + Subtitle adds a supporting line, and Image + Title + 2 Subtitles shows all four text layers. The headline, subtitle, and optional hero image — the words and lead visual that carry the screen. This guide documents every setting of the Content block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

The Content section holds the words on the screen: your headline, supporting text, or the question you ask the visitor. This is the copy that does the persuading, so write it like ad copy with one clear value proposition or one focused question per screen, and edit it before you touch colors or layout. It's available on most screens with editable text; media-only and pure paywall screens use their own copy areas instead.
Covered screen types: HeroContent, ListMultiPick, ListSinglePick, GridMultiPick, GridSinglePick, TextInput, WheelPicker, HeroList.

Rounds all four corners of the hero image; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer and more rounded. The default is 0. A small radius around 8 to 16 gives a modern, friendly look; match it to the rounding used elsewhere in your funnel, like buttons and cards, so the page feels consistent.

Sizes the hero image as a percentage of the screen height (0 to 100%), so it scales with the device, the more responsive way to size a hero. If set, it overrides any fixed height above. label: How a Flexible Layout screen works

Some Flexible Layout sections can read the visitor’s current Product Catalog selection. For a paywall, add a Product Catalog section, then link a Text section and a Purchase Button section to that catalog through each section’s “Linked to section” dropdown. The linked Text section can show the selected product description label, and the linked Purchase Button can show the selected product purchase label.

Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

Use + Add to choose what kind of block to place on this FlexibleLayout screen: text, media, product catalog, button, purchase button, list, custom embed, text field, spacer, header, footer, or paywall header. Add sections in the same order a visitor should read them, then drag to reorder if the screen flow changes. Start with the biggest structure first — for example header, hero text/media, products, and CTA — then tune layout settings inside each section.

Sets the color behind this section's content, used when the background type is Solid. The default is white. Enter a hex code or pick a swatch, and keep it in line with your theme so the screen feels on-brand, with enough contrast against the text on top to stay readable.

Sets what fills the area behind this section's content. Solid (the default) uses one color you pick below; Media places an image behind the content for a richer, ad-style look. If you go with Media and put text on top, keep the text readable with a darker image or an overlay so your value proposition doesn't get lost.

Sets the color of the section's outline. The default is black, and it only shows when the border thickness is above 0, so set a width first. Match it to one of your theme's accent colors for a clean, on-brand frame around the section.

Draws an outline around the section. The default 0 means no border; 1 to 2 pixels gives a subtle frame that makes a section read as a self-contained card or highlights an offer. Set this above 0 first, then pick the border color below.
Hex color for button background. Default yellow-gold (#ffc201). Primary visual element for call-to-action buttons.
Hex color for button border line. Only visible when border width is greater than 0.
Button border stroke width in pixels (0-50). Default 0 (no border). Used with border color for outlined button style.
Uniform corner radius (0-50 pixels) for all button corners. Default 12 creates slightly rounded button. Higher values create pill-shaped buttons.

Optional finishing touches for the button, such as overall transparency and entrance or tap animations. Use a subtle animation to draw the eye to a primary call-to-action, or lower the transparency to play down a secondary button. Leave it off for a plain, static button.

Optional. Layers a color gradient over the button's solid background for a richer, more premium look. Pick Simple (two colors), Medium (two colors plus a tilt angle), or Advanced (several color stops, with optional shimmer). Leave it off if a flat color is enough; turn it on to make a primary button catch the eye.

Adds a small image beside the button label, positioned left or right of the text, with controls for its size and surrounding spacing. Use a simple icon to reinforce the action — like an arrow on a 'Continue' button — and upload a transparent PNG or SVG so it sits cleanly. Leave it empty for a clean text-only button.

Sets the breathing room between the label or icon and the button's edges, set separately for top, bottom, left, and right. More padding makes the button bigger and easier to tap; too little makes it look cramped. Generous top and bottom padding gives a primary button a comfortable, finger-friendly tap area.

Optional. Casts a soft shadow beneath the button so it appears lifted off the screen, which helps a primary action stand out. Adjust blur for softness, spread for size, opacity for strength, and offset for direction. A subtle shadow usually looks best; leave it off for a flat, minimal style.
Text alignment within button: start (left in LTR), center, or end (right in LTR). Center alignment is typical for buttons.
Hex color for button label text. Default black (#000000). Must contrast with button background for readability.

Picks the typeface used for the button label. Leave it on your theme default so the button matches the rest of your funnel — mixing fonts on one screen looks unpolished and can hurt trust. Only override it when your brand requires a specific font.

Sets how large the text on the button appears. Most buttons read well at 16-18; go larger to make a primary action more prominent, but watch that the label doesn't wrap or overflow on small phone screens. Keep it consistent across your buttons so the screen looks intentional.

Sets how thick the button text is, from 400 (regular) through 700 (bold) and beyond. Bolder text draws the eye, so use 600-700 for a primary action you want people to tap. Keep lighter weights for secondary or less important buttons.

Sets the vertical gap between lines when a button label is long enough to wrap onto two or more lines. Most buttons use a single short label, so the default is fine and you can ignore this. Nudge it up only if a multi-line button looks cramped or hard to read.

The text shown on the button (placeholder 'Button Text'). Use a short, action-led phrase like 'Continue', 'Get Started', or 'Next' so people know exactly what tapping does. If your funnel runs in more than one language, this wording is saved per language, so set it for each one you support.

label: Space around the whole section stack

properties.summary: Container padding adds space between the phone edges and all sections on the screen. It is different from Section padding: container padding moves the entire stack inward, while section padding adds space inside one selected section. Use container padding first when every block feels too close to the screen edge, then use per-section padding only where a specific block needs more breathing room.

Rounds all four corners of the section. The default 0 keeps them sharp and square; higher values (try 8 to 16) give a soft card look that pairs well with a solid background or border to make the section stand out as its own block. The range is 0 to 50 pixels.

Use the trash icon to remove a section from the screen. Deleting also removes that section's content and can affect buttons linked to it, so confirm only after checking the preview and any parent-section links. If you are unsure, rename the section first or move it lower in the order while you verify the layout instead of deleting it immediately.

Controls how much leftover vertical space a section soaks up so the screen has no awkward gap. 0 keeps a section at its natural size (the default for text and buttons); 1 or more lets it stretch, and a section set to 2 takes twice the extra space as one set to 1. Raise this on your image or hero section to push the button down to a comfortable spot. Only applies when the section isn't set to scroll.

label: Let it shrink on small screens

properties.summary: Controls which section gives up height first when everything can't fit on a small phone. Higher numbers shrink sooner; 0 means never shrink this one. The default of 1 lets sections shrink evenly. Set 0 on must-stay pieces like the button or logo, and raise it on a less important section like a tall image, so the key content survives intact on the smallest screens.

Decides how the section's height is calculated. Auto (the safe default) makes it exactly as tall as its content, which is right for most text and buttons. Fixed lets you type an exact pixel height, and Percent sets it to a share of the screen, handy for a hero image that should always fill, say, the top 40 percent. Your pick also decides which value box below applies.

This is the number that pairs with your height mode. With Fixed mode, type pixels (0 to 1000, for example 320 for a tall hero); with Percent mode, type a share of the screen (0 to 100, for example 40). The box is ignored in Auto mode. For a scrollable section, this also sets the visible window the content scrolls inside.

Positions the content along the section's width: Left, Center, or Right. Center is the usual choice for headlines and buttons, while Left reads more naturally for longer body copy. (Left and right follow text direction, so they flip on right-to-left languages.)

label: Link the Purchase Button to the same catalog

properties.summary: Use the Purchase Button’s “Linked to section” dropdown to select the same Product Catalog section. This keeps the CTA tied to the visitor’s selected plan instead of a fixed product.

Some Flexible Layout sections can read the visitor’s current Product Catalog selection. For a paywall, add a Product Catalog section, then link a Text section and a Purchase Button section to that catalog through each section’s “Linked to section” dropdown. The linked Text section can show the selected product description label, and the linked Purchase Button can show the selected product purchase label.

Margin is the gap outside a section, between it and the sections next to it. Set Top, Bottom, Left, and Right independently, using positive values to push sections apart. A negative top margin pulls a section up so it overlaps the one above — for example, a headline resting on a hero image; pair that with stacking order to control what sits in front.

label: Text below or over the image

properties.summary: Decides whether your text and buttons sit below the image or float on top of it. Below media keeps content in its own space under the image — the safest choice for readability. Overlapping media lets the headline drift over the lower part of the image for a magazine-style hero; if you use it, add an overlay or gradient so the text stays legible against the picture.

Rounds the corners of the image or video. The default 0 is square; try 8 to 16 for a soft, modern look or a higher value for a strongly rounded card. Match it to the rounding on nearby buttons and sections so the whole screen feels cohesive.

Adds a dark fade over the bottom of the image or video so text placed on top stays readable. It's strongest at the bottom and clears toward the top. The default is black, which is the usual choice (or a dark brand color). Use it whenever you let content overlap the media so your headline and button don't get lost in a busy image.

label: How much height the image takes

properties.summary: Sets how much of the section's height the image or video fills, as a percentage. The default 50 splits the space evenly and leaves the lower half for your headline and button. Raise it (around 70) for a bold, image-led screen, or lower it when you need more room for copy and a clear call to action.

For video media only: turn on to loop the clip continuously, or leave off to play it once and stop. Looping suits short, ambient hero or background videos that keep the screen feeling alive, while play-once suits a clip with a clear start and finish. It has no effect on still images.

label: How the image fills its area

properties.summary: Decides how your image or video fits the section. Fill covers the whole area and crops the edges that don't fit — best for full-bleed hero shots and the right pick for most ad creatives. Fit shows the entire image but may leave blank bars around it; use it when nothing can be cropped. Stretch forces an exact fit but distorts the picture, so avoid it for photos.

label: Where the image starts on screen

properties.summary: Sets the top edge of your image or video. Screen Top runs it all the way up behind the status bar and header for a full-bleed, edge-to-edge hero. Header Bottom starts it just below the header bar so a back button or progress bar stays clearly visible. Pick Screen Top for an immersive opener, Header Bottom when the header needs to read cleanly.

Click the gear inside a section card to open that section's own settings. The first panel controls the section container — height, flex, scrollability, background, borders, alignment, padding, and margin — and the panel below controls the section's content, such as text, media, products, or button styling. This is the main place to tune how one block looks and behaves.

Padding is the space inside a section, between its edges and the content sitting in it. Set Top, Bottom, Left, and Right independently, starting from 0. Add some so text and buttons don't crowd the section border or a background image; 16-24 px all around is a comfortable, readable starting point.
Hex color for purchase button background. Default yellow-gold (#ffc201). Distinguishes purchase action from regular navigation.

Sets the color of the outline around the purchase button. It only shows up when the border thickness is above 0, so set a thickness first. Use it to give an outlined-style call-to-action a clean, contrasting edge.

Sets how thick the outline around the purchase button is, from 0 to 50 pixels. The default is 0, meaning no border; set a value together with a border color to create an outlined button. A solid filled button usually converts better, so most paywalls leave this at 0.

Rounds all four corners of the purchase button by the same amount, from sharp to fully rounded (0-50). The default of about 12 gives a softly rounded look; raise it toward 50 for a pill-shaped button, or set 0 for crisp square corners. Match it to your other buttons so the paywall feels cohesive.

label: Offer a cheaper plan on cancel

properties.summary: Controls what happens when someone cancels the payment. When on, they're sent to a downsale screen offering a cheaper or alternative plan — a second chance to recover the sale. When off, cancelling just sends them back with no further offer. Only turn this on if you've actually built a downsale screen in the funnel, otherwise there's nothing for it to open.

Optional finishing touches for the purchase button, such as overall transparency and entrance or tap animations. A subtle pulse or scale animation can pull attention to your call-to-action and lift conversions. Leave it off for a static button.

Optionally lays a color gradient over the button's solid background for a richer call-to-action. Pick Simple (two colors), Medium (two colors plus an angle), or Advanced (multiple color stops, with an optional shimmer). Use it to make your main CTA pop; leave it off if a flat color already stands out.

Optionally shows a small image next to the button label, to the left or right of the text. Upload an icon, then set its size and the spacing around it. A lock or arrow icon can reinforce the action, but a clean text-only button works just as well.

Sets the breathing room between the label or icon and the purchase button's edges, set separately for top, bottom, left, and right. More padding makes the button taller and easier to tap; too little looks cramped. Generous top and bottom padding helps your main purchase button feel substantial and inviting to press.

Optionally adds a soft shadow beneath the button so it lifts off the screen and pulls the eye toward your call-to-action. You can tune the softness (blur), size (spread), strength (opacity), and direction (offset). A subtle shadow usually works best; leave it off for a flat design.

Sets where the label sits inside the button: start (left in left-to-right languages), center, or end (right). Center is the standard choice and is recommended for a call-to-action so the label reads as one clear, balanced action.

Sets the color of the words on your purchase button. Make sure it contrasts strongly with the button background so the label stays easy to read — for example, dark text on the default yellow-gold button. Weak contrast means users miss the action, which directly costs you conversions.

Picks the typeface for the purchase button label, such as SF Pro or Helvetica. Match it to the rest of your paywall so the call-to-action looks intentional rather than out of place. Leave it on the theme default unless your brand uses a specific font.

Sets how big the label on your purchase button looks, measured in points. Since this is your main paywall call-to-action, keep it large and unmistakable — around 17 to 20 pt works well on most screens. Avoid going so big that the text wraps or spills outside the button on smaller phones.

Controls how thick or bold the button label appears, on a scale from 400 (regular) to 700 (bold) and heavier. As your primary call-to-action it should look bold and confident — a weight of 600 to 700 helps it visually dominate any secondary buttons on the screen.

Controls the vertical gap between lines when the button label runs onto two or more lines. Most call-to-action labels fit on one line, so you can leave this on the default. Adjust it only if a longer label looks cramped or too loose when it wraps.

The text on your paywall's purchase button (default 'Subscribe Now'). This is the most important call to action in the whole funnel, so make it clear and benefit-led, such as 'Start My Free Trial' or 'Unlock Full Access'. If you run multiple languages, this wording is saved per language, so translate it for each.

Drag the handle beside a section name to change the vertical reading order on the screen. The order here is the order visitors see in the preview and published flow, so keep the persuasion sequence clear: context first, offer/details next, then the CTA. After reordering, recheck fixed-height and flex settings because a section that worked in one position may need different spacing in another.

The Options section defines the answer choices, product cards, or tappable rows a visitor picks from on a selection screen. This is the core interaction that captures what the visitor wants, so pair it with Variable Binding to save each choice and use it to personalize copy and send the visitor toward the right paywall. Sets each grid cell's height as a percentage of its width: 100 is square, above 100 makes taller cells, below 100 makes wider, shorter cells. On grid cells, show or hide the selection checkbox and place it in a corner (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, or bottom-right) with an optional offset. Appearance of the selection checkbox — shape (square or circle), checked color, unchecked color, and padding. Use your theme's accent for the checked color so a tap reads clearly as selected, matching the selected-item look. Circle suits pick-one (radio style), square suits multi-select. Choose whether choices stack in a single-column list or sit in a two-column grid. Use a list for text-heavy answers that need a full line each; use a grid when items have images or icons and you want a compact, visual picker. On grid cards that show an image, this sets the image region as a whole: where it sits in the card, how tall it is (a fixed height or sized to fit its content), and the spacing around it. This shapes the image's container only; the image's own size and corners are set separately in the item image styles.

The spacing between adjacent choices — a vertical gap in lists, the gap between cells in grids. Around 8–12px keeps items clearly separate and easy to tap without wasting space. Increase it for a more airy feel, or decrease it to fit more options above the fold.

Adds the X in the header that lets people dismiss the paywall and keep browsing. properties.summary: How long the close button stays hidden (1-30 seconds) when you've set it to appear after a timer; it has no effect otherwise. Sets the color of the X dismiss icon (default white; applies only when the close button is shown). Controls when the X becomes tappable: right away, or after a short timer that lets users take in the offer first (set the length in the delay field below). The paywall's featured image or video — its source, how it fills its area, height, corner rounding, spacing, where it sits relative to the header and body, and an optional dark fade overlay for text readability. This guide documents every setting of the Paywall Media block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

The Paywall Media section is the featured image or video at the top of the paywall that visually sells the offer — a product shot, before/after, or short demo. Choose Image or Video and upload your asset, then check the preview so it reinforces the promise without pushing the plan cards and purchase button out of view on a phone. A relevant, high-quality visual builds trust, while an irrelevant one just wastes screen space.
Covered screen types: Paywall.

Sets how the media and the paywall text relate vertically. 'Above Content' keeps the media as a banner with the title, subtitle, and plans stacked below it (safest, always readable); 'Behind Intro Content' layers the title over the media for a magazine-style hero. Start with Above Content; if you choose the overlaid look, turn on the gradient overlay so the text stays legible.

Sets how rounded the corners of the image or video are. Zero gives sharp edges, which often look best for a full-width hero, while higher values give a soft, card-like look that matches rounded buttons and plan cards. Match it to the rest of your theme's rounding; the default is usually fine.

Turn this on to show a featured image or video at the top of the paywall, or off to hide media and give the plan cards more room. After enabling, choose the media type and upload your asset, otherwise nothing appears. Use media when a visual strengthens the offer; skip it for a tighter, text-only paywall.

Sets the color of the dark fade laid over your media (default black). Black works best behind white text; choose a dark brand color if you want the fade to feel on-theme. The overlay always fades to clear at the top, so only this base color matters. It appears only when the gradient overlay is turned on.

How far up the media the dark fade reaches, as a percentage. A low value shades only the bottom edge (enough for text sitting near the bottom); a high value darkens most of the image. Set it just high enough to cover where your overlaid text sits, leaving the rest of the image visible. This only appears when the gradient overlay is turned on.

Lays a dark fade over the image or video so any text and buttons placed on top stay readable. Turn it on whenever you layer the headline or content over the media, or when a busy or light image makes text hard to read; leave it off for a clean image with nothing on top. Once on, you can fine-tune its height and color below.

How much of the screen the featured image or video takes up, as a share of screen height. Keep it moderate (around 30 to 45%) so the plan cards and purchase button stay visible without scrolling; too tall pushes your offer below the fold and costs you sales. Always check the result on a phone-sized preview.

Upload (or clear) the hero image shown at the top of the paywall. Use a high-resolution image with its subject centered, since the edges may be cropped depending on your fit setting. If your funnel runs in multiple languages you can upload a different image per language; it appears only when media type is Image, and nothing shows until you upload one.

Picks whether the featured media is an image or a video. Image is simplest and loads fastest; video can show your product in motion but should be short and auto-playing. Note that switching type clears any asset you already uploaded, so choose first, then upload; picking Video also unlocks the loop option.

Sets the space between the media and its surroundings on each side: top, right, bottom, and left. Add padding to inset the image or video from the screen edges for a framed look, or set it to zero for a full-bleed, edge-to-edge hero. The theme default is a safe start; adjust only if the media looks too tight or too floaty in preview.

When on, the featured video repeats continuously; when off, it plays once and stops on the last frame. Loop short, ambient clips (a few seconds) so the paywall stays lively and eye-catching; turn it off for a video with a clear ending you don't want replayed. This only appears when the media type is Video.

label: How the media fills its area

properties.summary: Decides how your image or video sits in its space. 'Fit' shows the whole asset but may leave blank bars around it; 'Fill' crops the edges so the area is covered with no gaps. Fill usually looks best for a clean edge-to-edge hero, just keep anything important away from the edges; choose Fit only when the entire image must stay visible.

Sets where the image or video begins at the top of the screen relative to the header (back button and progress bar). 'Screen Top' starts media at the very top behind the header for a full-bleed hero look; 'Header Bottom' starts it just under the header so the controls stay clear of the image. Use Header Bottom if the header overlaps your media awkwardly, otherwise Screen Top is the most immersive.

Upload (or clear) the hero video shown at the top of the paywall. Keep it short and lightweight (a few seconds, compressed) so it loads fast on mobile data, and remember it auto-plays muted, so the visual must work without sound. If your funnel runs in multiple languages you can upload a different video per language; it appears only when media type is Video, and nothing shows until you upload one.

A floating bar pinned to the bottom of a Flexible Layout screen so the main button stays visible and tappable while content scrolls — its background bar (colour, opacity, corner radius, outline), the spacing from the edges and around the button, and whether it holds a standard or purchase button. This guide documents every setting of the Sticky Container block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

The Sticky Container pins one call-to-action button to the bottom of the screen so it stays visible while the visitor scrolls long content. Turn it on for screens where the next-step or buy button would otherwise scroll out of view — long sales copy, feature lists, the paywall — because keeping the button always tappable is one of the simplest ways to lift click-through on paid traffic. Leave it off on short screens that fit without scrolling, where it just adds clutter.
Covered screen types: FlexibleLayout.

Sets the color of the bar behind the pinned button (appears only when the bar is shown; defaults to white). Match it to your screen or theme background so the bar feels built-in, and make sure it contrasts with the button so the CTA stays the most eye-catching thing on screen. That contrast is what keeps the call-to-action obvious to paid-traffic visitors.

Sets the color of the bar's outline (defaults to black; appears only when the outline thickness is above 0 and the bar is shown). Pick a color that frames the bar without competing with the button — a subtle, theme-matched tone usually works best, keeping attention on the CTA itself.

Sets how thick the outline around the bar is, in pixels (default 0, meaning no outline; only applies when the bar is shown). Add an outline when the bar's color is close to the screen background and you want a crisp edge that separates the CTA from content behind it. Once it is above 0, the border color setting appears so you can style the outline.

Opens an inline card to set everything about the pinned button: its label, where it goes (next screen, or for a purchase button, which product it buys), icon, colors, fonts and shadows. The two things that move conversion most are setting the action correctly so the CTA actually leads somewhere, and writing a short benefit-driven label like 'Start free trial'. Style it to stand out clearly against the bar so it stays the obvious next step.

Chooses the pinned button's job: a standard button navigates to the next screen (use it on flow steps like 'Continue'), while a purchase button starts checkout and ties into your paywall products (use it on the paywall). The bar holds one button at a time, so switching type replaces it with a fresh default — your bar styling is kept, but you'll need to re-set the button's label and action.

Sets how rounded the bar's corners are, in pixels (default 12, only applies when the bar is shown). The default looks good on most screens; raise it for a softer, pill-like bar or set it to 0 for sharp corners. Match it to your buttons and cards so the bar looks like part of the design rather than an add-on.

The free-text input field — what kind of value it accepts and how typed answers look. This guide documents every setting of the Text Field block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

The Text Field section turns a screen into a question that collects a free-text answer such as a name, email, or goal. Set the placeholder hint, validation, and styling here; the answer is saved in a variable you can later use to branch the flow or personalize copy. Use it whenever the visitor should type an answer rather than pick from options — that captured input is what makes the screen gather usable data.
Covered screen types: TextInput.
When enabled, the field automatically receives focus and opens the keyboard when the screen appears. Default is true. Useful for primary input fields.

Sets the fill color inside the input box. Most funnels leave it clear so the screen background shows through, or use a subtle light fill to make the tappable field stand out. Just make sure it contrasts with the typed-text color so answers stay easy to read and people don't abandon the question.

Sets the color of the field's outline, which only appears when the Border Style is an underline or a full box. Use a tone from your theme — an accent or a soft neutral — so the field's edges read clearly as something to tap and type into. A visible outline helps people recognize and fill in the field.

Sets the gap OUTSIDE the field, separating it from the title above and anything below, on the top, right, bottom, and left. Use it to give the field room to breathe within the screen. This is the space around the field — distinct from Internal Padding, which is the space inside it.

Chooses how the field is outlined: a bottom underline under the text, a bottom underline with room for an icon, or a full box around the whole field. A full box reads most clearly as a place to type, while underline styles feel lighter. Your pick here also decides whether the Border Color and Border Width settings actually show.

Controls how thick the field's outline is, from 0 to 50 pixels (default 1). Keep it at 1-2 pixels for a clean, modern look and only go thicker for a deliberately bold style. A visible but restrained outline helps people spot the field at a glance and answer faster.

Sets a fill color behind the validation error message that appears when an answer is rejected. Usually leave it transparent so only the red text shows; add a subtle tint only if you want the error to read like a banner. Whatever you choose, keep enough contrast with the error text so the message stays readable and users can quickly fix and continue.

Sets the typeface for the validation error message shown when an answer is rejected. Leave it on your theme/system font unless you have a specific brand font, and match it to the field's font so the error looks like part of the same form. A consistent error style keeps the screen feeling polished and helps users trust and fix the field fast.

Sets the point size of the validation error message. Keep it a touch smaller than the field text (about 12-13pt) so it reads as a secondary note, but not so small it's hard to read on a phone. A legible error helps users spot and fix a rejected answer instead of abandoning the screen.

Sets how heavy the error message looks (for example 400 regular or 600 semibold). Regular (400) works in most cases; step up to 600 if you want the error to stand out more. Paired with the red color, a bit more weight helps users notice and correct a rejected answer so they keep moving through the funnel.
Message displayed when user input fails validation (does not match Validation Regex or Field Type). Shown to guide correction. Can be localized per locale.

Aligns the validation error message to the left, center, or right. Match it to the field's own text alignment (left is typical) so the message sits naturally under the input. Keeping them aligned makes it obvious which field was rejected, so users fix it quickly and don't stall.

Sets the color of the error text shown when an answer fails validation (default red, #FF3B30). Keep it red or another high-contrast warning color so people instantly see that their input was rejected and needs fixing. A clear error keeps them from giving up before they can continue.

Tells the field what kind of value to accept — plain text, a whole number, a decimal, a date, or an email — and automatically applies basic checks plus the right phone keyboard. Use Email for email capture and plain text for open answers. Picking the correct type blocks bad data, keeping any branching, analytics, or CRM that reads this answer reliable.

Picks the font used for both the placeholder hint and what the visitor types. Leave it on the system font unless you have a brand font, and match whatever the rest of your funnel uses. Consistent type keeps the page feeling polished and trustworthy, which matters when you're paying for the traffic.

Sets how large the text in the field appears, from 0 to 50 points (default 15). Keep it around 15-17 points so answers are comfortable to read on a phone. Text that's too small is hard to read on mobile, where most ad traffic lands, and can quietly drag down completion.

Sets how heavy the field text looks, from light (300) to bold (700), with regular (400) as the default. Regular is right for almost every input field. Keeping it regular makes the text read like an editable answer rather than a heading, so the field stays obvious and easy to use.

Rounds the corners of the icon image (0-50px, default 0 for square). Leave it at 0 for normal line or glyph icons; raise it only for a photo or avatar-style icon you want to soften or make circular. It has little visible effect on transparent line icons, so most fields can skip it.

Sets the horizontal space between the field's icon and the text the visitor types (default 8 pixels). The default works for most fields — nudge it up a little if the icon and text feel cramped, or down for a tighter look. The goal is an icon and placeholder that sit comfortably balanced.

Sets how tall the icon beside the input is (0-500px). Keep it around 20-24px so it lines up with the text, and usually match it to the icon width so the glyph stays square and undistorted. A right-sized icon reads as a helpful cue rather than visual clutter.

Where this screen's answer is stored — the variable, the value each choice maps to, and optional scoring. This guide documents every setting of the Variable Binding block, grouped by area. Each setting matches a real control in the screen editor.

Variable Binding saves what the visitor chooses or types on this screen as a named value you can reuse later. That saved value is what lets you personalize the funnel: send visitors down different paths based on their answer, segment them in analytics, and pass their details to your paywall and Stripe checkout. Without a binding the answer isn't stored and can't influence anything later, so it appears on every screen that collects an answer.

Type a value for a new option on this variable and click Add; it joins the options list and the mapping table below. A shortcut that rebuilds this variable's options from the screen's current list or grid items so the stored values match what's on screen, handy after you've added or changed items and don't want to re-enter each option by hand. The hero is the large featured image at the top of a headline or wheel-picker screen, the picture that sells the screen at a glance. Turn it on, then upload a file or paste an image URL. Pick a high-quality, on-message visual (product, result, or lifestyle shot); on a paid landing page it is often the first thing a visitor sees. Sizing and position are set just below.

Rounds all four corners of the hero image; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer and more rounded. The default is 0. A small radius around 8 to 16 gives a modern, friendly look; match it to the rounding used elsewhere in your funnel, like buttons and cards, so the page feels consistent.
How rounded the image is

Optionally pin the hero image to a set height with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty to let the image keep its natural proportions from the width — best for most screens. Use a fixed height when you want a consistent banner size; to size by screen proportion instead, use 'Image height relative to container' below, which takes priority over this value.
Fixed image height

Sizes the hero image as a percentage of the screen height (0 to 100%), so it scales with the device, the more responsive way to size a hero. If set, it overrides any fixed height above. A common starting point is 30 to 50% for a prominent banner that still leaves room for your title and button below; leave it empty to size by proportions instead.
Size the image by screen

Optionally pin the hero image to a set width with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty in most cases — the image then sizes to the screen and stays responsive across devices, which almost always looks best on a landing page. Set a fixed width only when you need the image smaller than full-width or aligned to a specific size.

Default is Aspect Fit, which never distorts; switch to Aspect Fill when you want it edge-to-edge and don't mind some cropping.

The hero is the large featured image at the top of a headline or wheel-picker screen, the picture that sells the screen at a glance. Turn it on, then upload a file or paste an image URL. Rounds all four corners of the hero image; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer and more rounded. The default is 0. The hero is the large featured image at the top of a headline or wheel-picker screen, the picture that sells the screen at a glance. Turn it on, then upload a file or paste an image URL. Pick a high-quality, on-message visual (product, result, or lifestyle shot); on a paid landing page it is often the first thing a visitor sees. Sizing and position are set just below.

Rounds all four corners of the hero image; 0 is sharp and higher values (up to 50) make them softer and more rounded. The default is 0. Optionally pin the hero image to a set height with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty to let the image keep its natural proportions from the width — best for most screens. Sizes the hero image as a percentage of the screen height (0 to 100%), so it scales with the device, the more responsive way to size a hero. If set, it overrides any fixed height above. Optionally pin the hero image to a set width with the slider (0–500) or by typing a number. Leave it empty in most cases — the image then sizes to the screen and stays responsive across devices, which almost always looks best on a landing page. On headline screens, this sets where the hero image sits relative to your title and subtitle — above the text, below it, or beside it. Lead with your strongest element: image-on-top when the visual is the hook, text-on-top when the headline does the selling. A custom domain (for example funnel.example.com) swaps the generic Segmently link for your own brand. Verification has to succeed before the domain can serve your live funnel, so don't publish against it until the status is green.
